Most French Speakers Are African (Map Explained)

Most French speakers are African.

About 320 million people speak French, and only one in five lives in France. More than half live in Africa. The most populous French-speaking country is the Democratic Republic of Congo, and its capital Kinshasa is now bigger than Paris. By 2050, by some estimates, eight in ten French speakers will be African.

title: Northern Europeans Get Half Their DNA From the Steppe (DNA Map)
caption:
Northern Europeans Get Half Their DNA From the Steppe (DNA Map)

Northern Europeans get about half their DNA from the steppe.

Five thousand years ago herders called the Yamnaya lived on the grasslands north of the Black Sea. Then they moved west. In Germany, skeletons from 4,500 years ago already carry about three quarters steppe ancestry. Every European today is a mix of three peoples: hunter-gatherers, farmers from Anatolia, and steppe herders. In Norway the steppe share is around half; in Sardinia it is very small.

Hunter, farmer or herder: which are you most? 👇

For centuries Persian was the language of poets and courts from Central Asia to India, and more than 100 million people speak it today.

title: The Taíno Were Never Wiped Out (DNA Map)
caption:
The Taíno Were Never Wiped Out (DNA Map)

The Taíno were never wiped out.

They were the people who met Columbus in 1492. Within fifty years disease, slavery and war had destroyed their world, and for centuries the history books called them extinct. Then scientists tested Puerto Ricans: about six in ten carry DNA from a Native American mother. In 2018, DNA from a thousand-year-old Taíno tooth was matched to living Puerto Ricans. And hurricane, hammock, canoe and barbecue are all Taíno words.

Puerto Ricans, did you know? 👇

caption:
East Germany Was Slavic (Map Explained)

East Germany was Slavic.

Berlin, Leipzig, Dresden: none of those names is German. Leipzig means the place of the linden trees, Dresden the people of the forest, and Berlin most likely comes from a Slavic word for swamp. Slavic tribes settled the land east of the Elbe about 1,400 years ago. From the 12th century German settlers moved east, and over generations the Slavs became Germans. One group never switched: about 60,000 Sorbs still live in eastern Germany.

Is your town's name Slavic? 👇

One family of languages covers almost half of Africa.

From Cameroon to Kenya to South Africa, hundreds of languages are cousins: Swahili, Zulu, Shona, Kikuyu, Lingala. They are the Bantu languages, and Bantu simply means people. About 4,000 years ago farmers began moving out of the borderland between Nigeria and Cameroon, carrying their crops and their language. By about 1,700 years ago they had reached South Africa. More than 300 million people speak a Bantu language today.

In 1928 young nationalists pledged one homeland, one nation, one language, and they picked Malay over Javanese, the biggest language by far. Most Syrians are not Arabs. They speak Arabic, but their roots are far older. Over 4,000 years ago Ebla and Mari were great trading cities here, and Damascus is one of the oldest cities still lived in. The Arameans settled Syria around 1100 BC, and their language, Aramaic, spread across the Middle East. Assyrians, Persians, Alexander and Rome all ruled here, then in 636 the Arab armies won at Yarmouk. The French aren't even French. Their name comes from the Franks, a Germanic tribe. Their language is Latin; their ancestry mostly isn't. Caesar conquered Gaul, Latin slowly replaced Gaulish and became French, but Rome sent governors and soldiers, not a new population. Pakistan isn't really a word. It's an acronym. In 1933 a Cambridge student, Choudhry Rahmat Ali, published a pamphlet called Now or Never and built a name from the Muslim provinces of the north-west: P for Punjab, A for Afghania (the North-West Frontier), K for Kashmir, S for Sindh, and TAN from Baluchistan. It also happens to mean "land of the pure" in Persian and Urdu. In 1947 the name became a country, and today over 240 million people carry it. Did you know? 👇

Most Algerians Aren't Arabs (Map Explained)

Most Algerians are not Arabs. Their ancestors are the Amazigh, the people the Romans called Berbers, who lived here thousands of years before Islam. Numidia's king Masinissa ruled from Cirta, today's Constantine, and Saint Augustine was born in Thagaste. Arab armies brought Islam and Arabic in the 600s, but far fewer people arrived than already lived here, and most Algerian ancestry is still North African. Since 2016, Tamazight is official again. Are Algerians Arabs? 👇

What Did the Romans Call Your City? (Map Explained)

What did the Romans call your city? London was Londinium, and nobody knows what it means. Paris was Lutetia, Cologne was Colonia (Köln literally means colony), Lisbon was Olisipo, Milan was Mediolanum and Budapest was Aquincum. And York was Eboracum, probably the place of the yew trees, which became Jorvik, then York, and gave its name to New York. What did the Romans call your city? 👇

Etymologies: Mediolanum and Eboracum are Celtic in origin; the Ulysses founding of Olisipo is a Roman-era legend. Elevation: AWS Terrain Tiles. Lithuania Was Once Europe's Biggest Country (Map Explained)

Lithuania was once the biggest country in Europe. The last pagans in Europe survived crusade after crusade from the Teutonic Knights, then expanded until, under Vytautas the Great, the Grand Duchy stretched from the Baltic to the Black Sea, over 800,000 km². In 1410 Lithuanian and Polish armies crushed the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald. Today Lithuania is about a twelfth of that size. Was Lithuania Europe's forgotten superpower? 👇

The Hidden World Under the Colosseum (3D Explained)

The Colosseum had a whole world hidden under the sand 🦁

The hypogeum was two floors of tunnels, cages and lifts. Teams of men turned wooden capstans to haul cages up to trapdoors in the arena floor, so a lion could appear out of nowhere in front of 50,000 people.

Up top, sailors from the navy rigged the velarium, a giant canvas roof against the sun. And ancient writers say the arena was flooded for mock sea battles before the tunnels were built.

Would you have bought a ticket? 👇

Australia Is Named After a Continent That Never Existed (Map Explained)

Australia is named after a continent that never existed. For centuries European maps showed a giant Terra Australis that nobody had seen. The Dutch called the real continent New Holland, Aboriginal people had lived there for over 50,000 years, and in 1803 Matthew Flinders sailed right round it and pushed for the name Australia. By 1824 it was official. Antarctica, the real southern land, wasn't even seen until 1820. Should it have stayed New Holland? 👇

caption:
France Brought Twice the Men to Agincourt. Mud Killed Them. (Battle Breakdown)

France brought twice the men to Agincourt. Mud killed them.

October 1415: Henry V's army was sick, starving and cut off from Calais. He chose a freshly ploughed field, soaked by a night of rain and squeezed between two woods. When the French refused to attack, he pulled up his stakes and marched into bow range. Cavalry broke on the stakes. Knights on foot sank with every step, packed so tight they could not raise their swords, and many suffocated without a wound. Then the archers dropped their bows and waded in with mallets.

Which battle should I break down next? 👇

caption:
Poland Vanished From the Map for 123 Years (Map Explained)

Poland vanished from the map for 123 years.

In 1771 Poland-Lithuania was one of the biggest countries in Europe. Then its three neighbours carved it up: Russia, Prussia and Austria took a slice each in 1772, Russia and Prussia came back in 1793, and in 1795 all three divided what was left. Poles kept their language and rose up in 1830 and again in 1863. In 1918 all three empires fell in the same war, and Poland walked straight back onto the map.

Would your country have survived that? 👇

caption:
Alexander the Great Was Not From North Macedonia (Map Explained)

Alexander the Great was not from North Macedonia.

He was born in Pella, which is in Greece, and the heart of ancient Macedon lies inside modern Greece. The Slavs who became today's Macedonians arrived about 900 years after he died. But Macedonia is also a region: in 1913 it was cut in three, with Greece taking about 51%, Serbia 38% and Bulgaria 10%. In 1991 the northern piece became a country called Macedonia, Greece blocked it from NATO in 2008, and in 2019 it became North Macedonia.

Who really owns the name? 👇

Only Turkey Recognises This Country: Northern Cyprus (Map Explained)

One third of this island is a country that only Turkey recognises.

Cyprus became independent from Britain in 1960, with about four in five people Greek Cypriot and one in five Turkish Cypriot. In 1974 Greek officers staged a coup to unite the island with Greece. Five days later Turkey invaded and took the northern third, and about 200,000 people fled across the line. The north declared itself a country in 1983; only Turkey recognises it. A United Nations buffer zone still cuts the capital, Nicosia, in half.

One country or two? 👇

A man born here in 1870 changed country four times without ever moving house.

Alsace and part of Lorraine were French in 1870, German from 1871, French again in 1918, annexed by Germany in 1940 and French again in 1945. Most people there spoke a German dialect the whole time. Today its capital, Strasbourg, is home to the European Parliament.

title: Transylvania Was Not Romanian Until 1918 (Map Explained)
caption:
Transylvania Was Not Romanian Until 1918 (Map Explained)

Transylvania was not part of Romania until 1918.

For most of the 900 years before that it belonged to the Kingdom of Hungary. But by the 1910 census Romanians were about 54% of the population and Hungarians about 32%. In 1918 Transylvania's Romanians declared union with Romania, and in 1920 the Treaty of Trianon made it official: Hungary lost about two thirds of its land. Around a million Hungarians still live in Romania today.

History or majority: which matters more? 👇
